# Voice Guide — Maya Torres

## Executive summary

Maya writes like an engineer filing a very confident bug report against the industry. Declarative, numbers-first, dry humor, zero hype. She never sells directly — she shows a cost table and lets the reader get angry on their own. Short posts; the longest thing she writes is still shorter than everyone else's.

## Core DNA

1. **Receipts over rhetoric.** Every claim ships with a number or a config snippet.
2. **Vendor-skeptic even though she's a vendor.** She critiques her own category, including herself.
3. **Deadpan, not snarky.** The joke is always in the understatement, never in an insult.

## The #1 rule

**Write like a post-mortem: what happened, what it cost, what we changed.** No adjectives doing load-bearing work.

## Top 10 posts (the evidence)

1. > "Our Datadog bill was $211k. Our revenue was $190k. I'll let you guess which line item survived the board meeting. (We don't have a board. The bill still didn't survive.)"
   — X, top post all-time. Why it worked: real number + deadpan turn in parentheses.
2. > "We turned off 71% of our alerts. Incidents went down. I have a theory and it's not a fun one."
   — X. Why it worked: counterintuitive stat + withheld conclusion pulls the click.
3. > "Pricing page or riddle? A thread on the 6 observability vendors whose cost I could not compute with a spreadsheet and a math degree."
   — X thread. Why it worked: names the enemy behavior, promises receipts.
4. > "Hot take: your on-call rotation isn't understaffed, your alerts are overconfident."
   — LinkedIn. Why it worked: reframe stated as a one-liner, no wind-up.
5. > "We're 9 people competing with a company that raised $400M. Our advantage: their sales team costs more than our payroll."
   — LinkedIn. Why it worked: David-vs-Goliath with an actual mechanism, not vibes.
6. > "I read all 47 pages of a competitor's pricing docs so you don't have to. Findings below. Bring a calculator and a priest."
   — X thread. Why it worked: does the reader's homework; "priest" is the only joke and it lands.
7. > "Log sampling is not data loss. Log sampling is admitting you were never going to read it."
   — X. Why it worked: aphorism form, engineer-true.
8. > "Month 1 of showing our full pricing math publicly: 3 competitors emailed me privately to say I'm crazy. Signups doubled. Both things can be true."
   — LinkedIn. Why it worked: experiment + result + wry acceptance.
9. > "The postmortem said 'human error.' The human was following the runbook. The runbook was wrong. Blame is a dependency graph."
   — X. Why it worked: escalating three-beat + a closing line that names the pattern.
10. > "We lost a deal to a vendor whose quote was 4x ours. Buyer said our price 'seemed too low to be enterprise-grade.' I've been laughing for three days."
    — LinkedIn. Why it worked: self-deprecating loss story that indicts the market, not the buyer.

## Hook formulas actually used

- **The two-number collision:** "$211k bill, $190k revenue" — two real figures that shouldn't coexist (posts 1, 5, 10).
- **The counterintuitive result, conclusion withheld:** "Alerts down 71%, incidents down. I have a theory." (post 2).
- **The homework flex:** "I read all 47 pages so you don't have to" (posts 3, 6).
- **The reframe one-liner:** no setup, thesis as first sentence (posts 4, 7).

## Content structures

- **Post-mortem arc:** what happened → what it cost (number) → what we changed → one dry line (posts 1, 8, 9).
- **Receipts thread:** claim → 4–6 evidence tweets, each standalone-quotable → no summary tweet (posts 3, 6).

## Language patterns

- **Sentence rhythm:** avg ~10 words; a fragment every 2–3 sentences; longest sentence rarely over 20 words.
- **Recurring phrases:** "I have a theory", "receipts below", "both things can be true".
- **Never uses:** "excited to announce", "game-changer", "thrilled", "🚀", "unlock", any word from a press release.
- **Punctuation:** parentheses for the joke; almost no em-dashes; no exclamation points, ever.
- **Profanity:** none on LinkedIn; rare single-word deployment on X for emphasis.

## Format-specific notes

### X
Standalone aphorisms or receipt-threads. Every thread tweet must survive being quote-posted alone. No "🧵" announcements.

### LinkedIn
First two lines carry the two-number collision (above the fold). Short paragraphs, no bold, no bullets. Ends flat and dry — never with a question to "drive engagement."
